metadata.file_name: 67. Anghel et al. (2024). The use of process data in large‑scale assessments: a literature review.pdf
metadata.title: The use of process data in large-scale assessments: a literature review

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a scoping review that synthesizes 221 empirical studies using process data in large-scale assessments; it does not analyze a student-level micro-dataset from PISA/TIMSS/NAEP/PIAAC. Because no respondent-level outcomes are estimated from an assessment dataset, there are no sampling weights, replicate weights, or weight variables to apply. The review’s “sample” is the set of included research articles identified through database searches and screening criteria, so weighting is not part of the statistical estimation procedure. Topic modeling was conducted on abstracts (not full papers), and the main methodological steps were text preprocessing and selecting the number of topics using semantic coherence and FREX.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because this is a literature review/scoping review that does not estimate cognitive achievement scores from ILSA plausible values. The dependent information is the presence and thematic content of process-data research as extracted from abstracts and coded from full papers, not PV-based student achievement.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The review followed Arksey and O’Malley’s scoping review framework. It searched Scopus, ERIC, and Google Scholar (May–June 2022) using Boolean keyword groups for process/log data and LSA contexts, then removed duplicates (4677 remaining). Screening retained English-language studies with empirical components that relied on at least one type of process data in an educational LSA, including studies using complex problem-solving (CPS) even when not directly in reading/math/science. It excluded non-LSA/non-process studies, non-empirical papers, conference proceedings, books/dissertations/technical reports (by volume), preprints/work in progress, non-English papers, and unavailable sources; 232 articles were retained initially, and 221 were included in the topic model after excluding 11 papers without abstracts.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict problem-solving, finding that This scoping review used structural topic modeling (STM) to identify recurring themes in 221 empirical studies that used process/log data in large-scale assessments. The review’s “inputs” were the abstracts of included papers (with citations/section headings removed and standard NLP preprocessing such as lowercasing, stopword removal, and stemming), and the “outputs” were topic assignments based on the highest posterior topic probability. The authors estimated STM models with 5–10 topics and selected a six-topic solution using semantic coherence and FREX, then manually coded subtopics and extracted theories/methods from full papers. The six recurring topics were response time models, response time-general, aberrant test-taking behavior, action sequences, complex problem-solving, and digital writing. The study does not report predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) because it is not training ML models on student outcomes; instead, it maps how process data are used and which theories are invoked, with limitations related to topic-model assignment ambiguity and the exclusion of papers without abstracts. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a scoping/literature review rather than an empirical ML study on student-level outcomes. Consequently, there is no student sample size, no country-level analytic sample, no PV-based achievement target, and no predictive model evaluation metrics to extract. The only ML-like component is topic modeling for literature theme extraction, which is not framed here as a supervised predictive task with a target variable and performance metrics.
